zh.title: 之二 · 我只剩一点疑虑
zh.deck: 阿尔诺指出一个循环；笛卡尔的回答，把读者领回这本书前面几处。

paragraphs: 这本书有一条反驳，后来有了自己的名字。它以循环这个名目说出来，是在这本书自己的第四组反驳里；同样的疑问，梅森那一组已经问过。两回都是作者收进书里的。

sections.heading: 那条反驳是什么
paragraphs: 先说它要打的是什么。
照阿尔诺的排法，笛卡尔在六个沉思里走的是这么一条路：凡是我清楚分明看见的，就是真的；我凭这一条证出神存在；而神不骗人，所以凡我清楚分明看见的确实是真的。
阿尔诺疑心这里转了个圈。他写：
我只剩一点疑虑，就是他怎么才算没有犯循环。他说我们之所以确知凡清楚分明所见为真，只因为神存在。可我们要确知神存在，又只因为这一点是我们清楚分明看见的。那么在确知神存在之前，我们就得先确知凡清楚分明看见的都是真的。
这段话后来有个名字，叫笛卡尔循环。三百多年过去，它还在被人讨论。

sections.heading: 说它的人，和印它的人
paragraphs: 要紧的是它出现在哪里。
不是后人翻出来的破绽。是付印之前要来的反对意见里的一条，作者收进书里，排在正文后面。
而且阿尔诺说得很客气。他不说我抓到一个漏洞，他说我只剩一点疑虑。全组反驳他先作哲学家说了一段，再作神学家说一段，这一条是哲学家那一段的收尾。
收完他还添了一句：再补一句刚漏掉的。跟着又提出一条新的：笛卡尔断定心灵里凡有的它都自知，这一点我看是错的；比如胎儿。
一条足以动摇全书的反驳，末尾接着一句顺手补的。这是被请来挑毛病的人的口气。

sections.heading: 他怎么答
paragraphs: 答在同一本书里，隔了几十页。
他的答法是切开：此刻正在清楚看见，和记得自己先前清楚看见过，这是两件事。
头一件不需要神。当你正盯着那几条理由看的时候，神存在这一条就立住了，靠的是你此刻在看。第二件才需要：过后你不再盯着看了，只剩一个记得。要让那个记得还算数，得有别的东西在底下托着。神托的是第二件，不是头一件；所以在他看来，圈没有转起来。
这个答案是不是够，本书不判。这里要看的是另一样。

sections.heading: 一套自己引自己的装置
paragraphs: 他答这一条的时候，写的是：这我在答第二组反驳的第三节和第四节里已经讲够了。
他没有重讲一遍，他指回这本书前面的一篇答辩。而那一篇答的，是梅森那一组早先提过的同一个疑问：您既然说确知神存在之前什么都确知不了，那您连自己是一个在思想的东西，都还不能确知；何况一个不信神的几何学者，照样清楚分明地知道三角形三个角等于两个直角。
答梅森的时候，他也没有新造什么。他说：这一点我在那里已经明明白白说过了，我讲的只是那些结论的确知，是我们不再盯着推出它们的理由，只剩下记得的那一种。那个那里，是第五个沉思。
所以这条路是这样走的。第五个沉思里先有这个分别；梅森问了一回，他指回沉思；阿尔诺换个说法又问一回，叫它循环，他指回答梅森的那一篇。同一个疑问被问了两回，他两回都往回指。
到这一步，这本书的摆法就清楚了。反驳和答辩不是一沓附录，它们跟六个沉思互相指着。他在书前就请读者，先把反驳和答复读完，再对沉思下判断。跳过去只读六个沉思，读到的是一本缺件的书。

sections.heading: 介绍人，和煤气
paragraphs: 阿尔诺指的那个圈，日常里也有。
打听一个人靠不靠谱，找个熟人问问，而那个熟人是他介绍给你的。这还不算圈，熟人可能真认识他。圈是这样的：你信这个熟人，只因为他说这熟人可靠；你信他，又只因为这熟人说他可靠。两头各靠对方撑着，中间没有第三样东西。
至于他那个切开的答法，日常里也有。
出门走出两条街，忽然想不起煤气关没关。你确实关了，而且关的时候是看着关的。可现在手上只剩一个记得。当时看着的那一眼，和此刻的这个记得，隔着的东西不是时间那么简单。有人会掉头回去，那是不认这个记得；有人接着走，那是认了。
笛卡尔要的，是让这个记得站得住。他在底下放了神。

sections.heading: 收束
paragraphs: 这个疑问，后人给它起了名字。
问它的有两组，把两回都印出来的是笛卡尔。没有摆在不显眼的地方，连阿尔诺那句客气的开场和顺手补上的下一条，都一并印着。
他答阿尔诺，指回答梅森的那一篇；那一篇又指回沉思。要读懂最后那个答案，得先读梅森那一条和他当时的答复。

notes: 对应第四组反驳及答辩、答第二组第三至第四节、第五沉思。本文转述笛卡尔区分当下直观与事后记忆的答法，不据此裁定“笛卡尔循环”已经解决。
介绍人与煤气的场景是本系列的说明性比喻，不是笛卡尔原书举的例子。
zh.aside: 《SAE第一批判》用过一把测试，找的是说出来就撤不掉的东西。阿尔诺用的是形状相近的另一把，指认的是辩护里预支了的结论。两把不是同一把；这是旁注，不是论证。

title.zh: 笛卡尔全集第七卷：读者序及第一至第五组反驳与答辩
title.en: Descartes, Œuvres VII: Preface and the Objections and Replies

coverage: 一套自己引自己的装置

en.title: One Doubt Remains
en.deck: The famous circle was not discovered behind the author’s back. He printed the objection himself.

paragraphs: One objection in this book acquired a name of its own. It appears as a charge of circular reasoning in the Fourth Objections. Mersenne’s group had already raised the underlying difficulty. Both exchanges are in the volume Descartes sent to press.

sections.heading: What is supposed to go in a circle?
paragraphs: Here is the route as Arnauld lays it out. Whatever I perceive clearly and distinctly is true. On that basis I establish that God exists. Since God does not deceive, what I perceive clearly and distinctly must indeed be true.

Arnauld wonders how Descartes avoids a circle. We are certain that clear and distinct perceptions are true only because God exists; yet we are certain of God’s existence only because we perceive it clearly and distinctly. Must we not already trust that kind of perception before establishing God?
The problem came to be known as the Cartesian Circle. It has outlived both men and remains a subject of philosophical dispute.

sections.heading: The person who objected, and the person who printed it
paragraphs: What matters here is where the objection appears. It was not an embarrassment dug up centuries afterwards. It arrived in a solicited report before publication, and the author placed it after his own main text.

Arnauld’s manner is courteous. He does not announce that he has caught a fatal error. He says one doubt remains. He has divided his report between philosophy and theology; this doubt closes the philosophical portion.
Then he adds something else he had nearly forgotten: Descartes’ claim that the mind is aware of everything within it seems wrong. Consider a child in the womb.
A challenge to the foundations of the argument is followed by an additional item almost as an afterthought. It is the voice of someone doing the job he was asked to do.

sections.heading: The distinction in the reply
paragraphs: Descartes answers within the same volume. He separates two conditions: attending to something clearly now, and remembering that one attended to it clearly before.

On his account, the first does not require an appeal to God. While the mind attends to the reasons establishing God’s existence, their evident force is present. The difficulty concerns what happens afterwards, when one is no longer considering the reasons and remembers having understood them.

That later confidence requires a guarantee. God is invoked for it, not to supply the immediate force of the original insight. In Descartes’ view, distinguishing the two prevents the supposed circle from closing.
Whether the answer succeeds is not decided here. There is something else to notice about how it is delivered.

sections.heading: A book that sends you back through itself
paragraphs: When he replies to Arnauld, Descartes says he has already explained the point sufficiently in the third and fourth sections of his response to the Second Objections. Rather than start over, he sends the reader to an earlier reply.

That reply answers a difficulty raised by Mersenne’s group. If nothing can be known with certainty before God’s existence is known, how can Descartes already be certain that he is a thinking thing? And what about an atheist geometer who clearly understands that a triangle’s angles equal two right angles?

Replying to them, Descartes again says he has already made the point clear. He means the certainty of conclusions remembered after their grounds are no longer before the mind. The earlier place he invokes is the Fifth Meditation.

The path therefore runs backwards. A distinction appears in the Fifth Meditation. Mersenne’s group challenges the position, and the reply points back to that distinction. Arnauld raises the difficulty again as a circle; Descartes points back to the answer he gave Mersenne.

These are not merely detachable appendices. Objections, replies and meditations refer into one another. The author has already asked us to read the exchanges before passing judgment on the main text. Skipping them means missing part of the argument the book asks us to assess.

sections.heading: A reference, and a gas tap
paragraphs: The alleged circle has an everyday counterpart. You ask whether someone is trustworthy and consult a reference they themselves supplied. That alone need not be circular: the reference may genuinely know them. The circle begins if you trust the referee only because this person recommends them, and trust the person only because the referee recommends them. Neither judgment has an independent support.

The distinction in Descartes’ answer also has an everyday counterpart. Two streets from home, you cannot remember whether you turned off the gas. You did turn it off, and watched yourself do so. But what you have now is a memory.

The difference between seeing the closed tap then and recalling it now is more than elapsed time. One person goes back because the memory does not settle the matter; another keeps walking because it does.
Descartes wants the later confidence to have a secure footing. Underneath it, he places God. The household example makes the distinction visible; it does not vindicate his guarantee.

sections.heading: At the end
paragraphs: Later readers gave the difficulty a name. Two groups asked it, and Descartes printed both. Arnauld’s courteous opening and his next, almost casual objection remain there too.
To answer Arnauld he directs us to Mersenne’s exchange; that exchange directs us to a meditation. Before judging the final answer, we have to follow the route by which it arrives.

en.aside: The SAE First Critique uses a test for claims that cannot be withdrawn in the act of making them. Arnauld’s test has a different task: identifying a conclusion already borrowed by the argument supposed to support it. The resemblance is a reason to compare them, not to treat them as the same test.
notes: Read the Fourth Objections, the corresponding Fourth Replies, sections III–IV of the Second Replies, and the Fifth Meditation together. The account distinguishes Descartes’ proposed answer from a judgment that it resolves the Cartesian Circle.
The examples of a personal reference and checking the gas are explanatory analogies, not historical examples used by Descartes.
